questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Explain an everyday design that accommodates expansion of a solid.
questions.prompt: A workshop fits a long metal sunshade with one end fixed and the other free to slide a short distance. Why is the sliding end useful on a hot afternoon?
questions.answer: It lets the metal lengthen without building up as much compressive stress.
questions.explanation: Heating makes the metal expand. The free end can move, reducing the tendency to buckle.
options: It keeps the metal at its morning temperature.
It lets the metal lengthen without building up as much compressive stress.
It stops the metal conducting thermal energy.
It makes the metal shorten when heated.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of heating a gas at fixed volume using particle collisions.
questions.prompt: A sealed rigid container of air warms in sunlight. Use the particle model to explain why the pressure rises while the container volume stays fixed.
questions.answer: The air particles gain kinetic energy, move faster, and strike the walls more frequently and with greater momentum changes. The greater force per unit area increases pressure.
questions.explanation: The container keeps the same gas and wall area. Faster particles transfer more momentum to the walls per unit time.

markingGuide.description: Explain that the particles move faster.
Link faster motion to more frequent or more forceful wall collisions.
Link the increased force on the same wall area to greater pressure.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Infer a specific heat capacity ratio from unequal masses and equal temperature rises.
questions.prompt: Two insulated blocks receive equal amounts of energy and each warms by 12 °C. Block A has mass 0.30 kg and block B has mass 0.45 kg. Assume the supplied energy goes only into the blocks. Find the ratio of the specific heat capacity of A to that of B.
questions.explanation: With the same energy and temperature rise, mc is the same for both blocks. Therefore cA/cB = mB/mA = 0.45/0.30 = 1.5.

markingGuide.description: Infer that the ratio of specific heat capacities is the inverse mass ratio.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Connect the escape of higher-energy particles to cooling.
questions.prompt: A pupil places a damp cloth over a sealed bottle. As water leaves the cloth by evaporation, the bottle cools. Which particle-level explanation describes the cooling of the water remaining in the cloth?
questions.answer: Faster particles escape, lowering the average kinetic energy of the remaining water particles.
questions.explanation: Evaporation preferentially removes more energetic particles from the surface, reducing the mean kinetic energy of those left.
options: The escaping particles make the remaining particles move faster.
Every remaining particle stops moving at once.
Water particles cool because they get smaller.
Faster particles escape, lowering the average kinetic energy of the remaining water particles.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Interpret absorption evidence to distinguish alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
questions.prompt: In a simulated shielding test, thin paper has little effect on the count from a source. A few millimetres of aluminium reduce it to background. Which single radiation type best fits the result?
questions.explanation: Paper would stop alpha radiation. The aluminium stopping the detected radiation is consistent with beta radiation and is less consistent with penetrating gamma radiation.
options: All three types are equally consistent with the result.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Subtract background count rate before identifying a half-life.
questions.prompt: A simulated counter records 104 counts/min at 0 min, 64 at 6 min and 44 at 12 min. The steady background is 24 counts/min. Determine the half-life and explain why halving the first uncorrected count rate would be misleading.
questions.answer: 6 min. The corrected rates are 80, 40 and 20 counts/min.
questions.explanation: Subtract 24 counts/min at each time. The source contribution halves every 6 min, while the background contribution stays constant.

markingGuide.description: Subtract the background and give the corrected rates.
Identify 6 min as the time for one halving.
Explain that the raw readings include a steady contribution.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Apply conservation of nucleon number and charge to a beta-minus equation.
questions.prompt: A sodium-24 nucleus (atomic number 11) emits a beta-minus particle. Give the mass number and atomic number of the daughter nucleus and explain the changes using the neutron-to-proton conversion.
questions.answer: Mass number 24 and atomic number 12. A neutron changes to a proton and an electron is emitted.
questions.explanation: Replacing one neutron with a proton keeps the total number of nucleons constant and adds one to the proton number.

markingGuide.description: Explain that one neutron becomes a proton in beta-minus decay.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish random individual decays from a predictable trend across many nuclei.
questions.prompt: A class simulation shows the number of undecayed nuclei dropping over time. A learner claims the curve can identify the exact next nucleus to decay. Explain what the curve can and cannot tell the learner.
questions.answer: The curve describes the overall decline in the number of undecayed nuclei. It cannot identify the next nucleus because individual decay is random.
questions.explanation: A large sample can show a reproducible trend even though individual nuclei decay spontaneously and unpredictably.

markingGuide.description: Recognise that the curve describes a sample-level trend.
Explain that individual decay is random, so the next nucleus cannot be identified.
